concept.title: Cascade and declarations
concept.shortdesc: A stylesheet is a list of rules, and several rules often apply to the same element. This chapter explains how CSSMedia decides which rule wins, how elements get values from their parents, and how to write less CSS with shorthands, custom properties and conditions. The cascade reference at the end lists the at-rules and media features.

conbody.p: A CSS rule has a selector and a list of declarations between braces. The selector says which elements the rule is for. Each declaration has a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon:

CSSMedia reads your stylesheets and applies them to your XML. It has almost no built-in rules of its own, so what you see in the PDF is what your rules say. A declaration that CSSMedia does not understand, because the property is unknown or the value is not valid, is ignored, and the other declarations still apply.

One element can match many rules, and two rules can set the same property with different values. The cascade is the set of steps that picks one value for each property of each element. It works on every property alone: one rule can win for color while another wins for margin.

The cascade picks a value when at least one rule sets the property. When no rule does, the element takes the value of its parent or the initial value of the property. After that, CSSMedia computes the final value. For example, it turns 2em into a length in pixels and replaces var() with the value of a custom property.
